assistant:
At **20:00 on 6 January**, Bus_29 was at **0.943 p.u.**, below the **0.950 p.u.** limit. The comparison point at **18:30**, just before the undervoltage began, was **0.952 p.u.** The measured change between those moments was a **0.009 p.u.** voltage drop.

The main driver was rising demand near Bus_29: demand at Bus_29 and Bus_28 increased by **1.18 MW** combined, accounting for **71.1%** of the drop. Bus_29’s own demand rose by **0.96 MW**. Demand elsewhere rose by **24.47 MW**, contributing **28.7%**. The five generators’ combined output fell by **5.73 MW**, but the investigation attributed only **0.2%** of the drop to unit output and ruled it out as a material cause. The measured changes showed no suspicious jumps.

This was part of a recurring pattern: Bus_29 had **12 undervoltage episodes** during the measured week; in all **10 episodes investigated**, demand was the main cause. The local-demand contribution was **70.6–71.6%**.

A preventive test found a warning at **18:30**, 15 minutes before the episode began. Raising Gen_bus7’s voltage set-point by **0.014 p.u.** from that warning was **not sufficient** to keep Bus_29 within limits throughout the episode; it also caused an overload on line **Bus_5 → Bus_7 [L9]**. Separately, an OPF found a feasible dispatch for the **20:00 snapshot** with Bus_29 at **0.950 p.u.** That is a result for that moment, not proof that the same dispatch would prevent the whole episode.

The study doesn’t establish *why* demand rose—weather, calendar effects, or a particular customer would require external weather or finer-grained demand data. It also doesn’t calculate a voltage-collapse margin, so proximity to collapse was not assessed. The measured-load reactive demand was derived using the default **0.95 lagging power factor**.

📋 Data source: measurements
